name: Thymosin alpha-1
summary: A 28-amino-acid immune-signaling peptide, sold abroad as Zadaxin mainly for hepatitis B and taken for immune support; FDA found the evidence insufficient for every use it reviewed.
what_it_is: Thymosin alpha-1 is a 28-amino-acid peptide that acts on the immune system; a synthetic form is sold as Zadaxin. Its maker reports approvals in several countries, mainly for chronic hepatitis B and as a helper for flu vaccines in people with weak immunity, but FDA could not verify these and has approved no thymosin alpha-1 product. People take it hoping to strengthen immune defenses.

evidence.why: Many human trials exist, but FDA judged the evidence insufficient for every use it reviewed, and the largest well-designed trial, in 1,106 adults with sepsis, found no effect on survival.

status_us.label: Not approved; FDA advisers voted against compounding
status_us.note: No thymosin alpha-1 product is FDA-approved, though it has four US orphan-drug designations; its compounding nomination was withdrawn, but FDA reviewed it anyway, and in December 2024 FDA's advisers voted 17-4 against adding it to the list pharmacies may compound from. FDA still cites possible immune reactions, and for outsourcing facilities it sits in Category 3 (nominated without adequate support).

benefits.claim: No clear survival benefit in sepsis: an earlier trial of 361 adults reported 26% vs 35% deaths at 28 days with no difference in ICU deaths, and a later placebo-controlled trial of 1,106 adults found no survival benefit (23.4% vs 24.1%)
Mixed results in chronic hepatitis B: in one placebo-controlled trial the virus became undetectable about as often as with placebo (20% vs 21%), and FDA found the evidence insufficient
Somewhat higher tumor response rates than control (6% to 12% vs 4%) in a 488-patient melanoma trial, but the difference was not statistically significant
Fewer COVID-19 deaths in one of four meta-analyses; the other three found no reduction

risks.risk: Injection-site irritation, redness or discomfort, the most commonly reported side effects
Possible immune reactions to the peptide or to impurities and clumps, which FDA could not rule out
Liver enzyme (ALT) flares in people with chronic hepatitis B and thyroid test (TSH) changes in people with hepatitis C were reported in trials
A fatal immune destruction of red blood cells in 1 of 6 stem-cell transplant recipients who also received donor immune cells; FDA could not tell whether thymosin alpha-1 contributed
FDA flagged safety concerns about use in transplant patients and alongside flu vaccines

avoid_if: Stem-cell transplant recipients (FDA flagged a fatal immune reaction and more infections after stem-cell transplant)
Chronic hepatitis B or C, unless a liver specialist is involved (liver flares and thyroid changes reported; approved antiviral drugs exist)
interactions: Flu vaccines: FDA raised safety concerns about using it as a vaccine helper and found too little evidence of benefit

before: Liver enzymes (ALT) and thyroid test (TSH), especially with viral hepatitis
during: Liver enzymes and TSH if used with viral hepatitis
labs.why: No evidence-based monitoring exists for thymosin alpha-1; liver enzyme flares and thyroid test changes were reported in hepatitis trials.

studies.title: The efficacy and safety of thymosin α1 for sepsis (TESTS): multicentre, double blinded, randomised, placebo controlled, phase 3 trial
studies.people: 1,106 adults with sepsis in 22 hospitals in China
studies.finding: Deaths within 28 days were 23.4% with thymosin alpha-1 and 24.1% with placebo, and no secondary or safety outcome differed. Possible differences by age and diabetes were called hypothesis-generating.

studies.title: FDA Evaluation of Thymosin Alpha-1 (Ta1) – Related Bulk Drug Substances (Ta1 (free base) and Ta1 acetate)
studies.people: Published human and animal studies, including trials in hepatitis, sepsis, cancer and COVID-19
studies.finding: FDA found too little nonclinical safety data, listed adverse events including liver enzyme flares, thyroid test changes and a fatal case after stem-cell transplant, and concluded the evidence weighed against allowing compounding.

studies.title: Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee Meeting: Thymosin Alpha-1 (Ta1) Related Bulk Drug Substances (FDA presentation)
studies.people: Trials in hepatitis B and C, sepsis, melanoma, liver cancer and COVID-19
studies.finding: FDA judged effectiveness insufficient for every use reviewed: hepatitis B results were mixed, a 488-patient melanoma trial showed no significant difference, and three of four COVID-19 meta-analyses found no effect on deaths.

ask_your_clinician: What is behind my concern about immunity, and which proven treatments or vaccines fit?
If I have hepatitis B or C, how does this compare with approved antiviral drugs?
Which side effects or lab changes should make me stop?

notes_for_editor: Main sources are FDA's evaluation memo (November 15, 2024) and FDA's presentation slides (December 4, 2024); the slide-deck title is descriptive. Other-country approvals of Zadaxin come from the manufacturer (a 2014 SciClone report and a product monograph), which FDA could not verify. FDA reports more than 4,400 trial participants, a figure from a review co-written by manufacturer employees. The earlier sepsis result (ETASS, 361 patients, 26% vs 35%) is as reported in FDA's slides; its design was not checked. NEXT_ROUND says the 503A nomination was withdrawn in September 2024; FDA's page lists it in the withdrawn table without a date. The 503B Category 3 listing is from FDA's March 21, 2025 list. WADA's 2026 list names thymosin beta-4 but not thymosin alpha-1. Round-1 notes (cjc1295) say the FDA Law Blog mentions a lawsuit involving thymosin alpha-1 with no reported outcome; not re-checked here.
